To reverse means to go against the current direction, order, or state of something — either by moving backward, flipping things around, or undoing what was done.

The word always carries one powerful idea: opposition to what currently is or what was moving forward.

1. To move in the opposite direction (especially backward)

This is the most physical sense. When something or someone reverses, they move in the direction opposite to the one they were going in — most commonly, backward.

  • "She reversed the car out of the parking spot." — She drove it backward.
  • "The wind reversed, now blowing from the east instead of the west." — The wind changed to the opposite direction.
  • "The army was forced to reverse its advance and retreat." — It turned around and moved back.

Notice that in some sentences, you reverse something (you act on an object), and in others, something just reverses on its own. Both are correct uses of this verb.

2. To flip the order or arrangement of something

Here, "reverse" means to put things in the opposite order — what was first becomes last, what was at the top goes to the bottom, what faced one way now faces the other.

  • "Reverse the list — I want the newest items at the top." — Flip the order so the last item becomes the first.
  • "He reversed the image so the text would read correctly in the mirror." — He flipped it horizontally.
  • "The situation reversed their roles — the student was now teaching the teacher." — Their positions swapped completely.

The key feeling here is that whatever the arrangement was, it has been turned exactly around.

3. To undo or cancel a decision, ruling, or action

This is a very common and important use. When a person, court, organization, or authority reverses a decision, they officially cancel it, invalidate it, and often restore what was in place before.

  • "The company reversed its decision to close the factory." — They cancelled that decision; the factory stays open.
  • "The appeals court reversed the original verdict." — The higher court overturned the lower court's ruling; the original outcome no longer stands.
  • "The government reversed the new policy after widespread protests." — They withdrew and cancelled the policy.

The implication is not just "they changed their mind" but specifically that they went back against what was previously decided or done.

4. To stop a process and make it go the opposite way (undo damage, change, or decline)

This is a subtler, very important sense. When you try to reverse a trend, a condition, or a process, you're trying to stop it from continuing in its current direction and push it back — often toward a healthier, better, or earlier state.

  • "The new medicine was able to reverse some of the damage to the patient's liver." — It didn't just stop the damage; it actually undid and repaired it.
  • "The country's leaders struggled to reverse the economic decline." — They worked to stop the downward spiral and push the economy back upward.
  • "Exercise cannot fully reverse the effects of aging, but it can slow them down." — It cannot completely undo those effects.
  • "The charity's efforts reversed the trend of increasing poverty in the region." — The trend was going in one direction (poverty rising); the efforts pushed it in the opposite direction (poverty falling).

This sense involves the idea of a process or trajectory — something has been moving in a direction, and to reverse it is to make it move the opposite way.

5. To reverse charges (a specific, fixed phrase)

In British English especially, "to reverse the charges" on a phone call means to call someone in a way where they pay for the call instead of you. The financial responsibility is flipped — moved in the opposite direction from the usual.

  • "He had no money, so he reversed the charges and his mother paid for the call."

This is a fixed, idiomatic phrase but follows the same logic: the direction of who bears the cost is flipped.

No matter which sense you're looking at, "reverse" always involves a turning-against, a going-backward, or a flipping-around of something that was established:

  • A car moving forward → made to go backward.
  • A list in one order → flipped into the opposite order.
  • A decision that stood → cancelled and undone.
  • A process heading in one direction → pushed to go the opposite way.
  • A caller paying → the receiver made to pay instead.

The verb can work with an object ("She reversed the car") or without one ("The car reversed") — both are grammatically natural.
A Few More Natural Examples Across Contexts

• "The tide reversed, and the water began rushing back out to sea."
  • "It is very difficult to reverse the effects of deforestation once it reaches a certain point."
  • "The referee reversed his call after reviewing the footage." — He changed the call to the opposite one.
  • "Years of therapy helped her reverse the negative thought patterns she had developed in childhood."
  • "The union's actions reversed the wage cuts that management had imposed." — The cuts were undone; wages went back up.

• Undo — Informal, general; suggests cancelling a previous action. "Reverse" is more formal and also covers direction and processes.
  • Overturn — Used specifically for decisions, rulings, and structures being toppled. "Reverse" overlaps here but is broader.
  • Invert — Means to flip upside down or inside out; more physical and spatial. "Reverse" can mean flip but also covers decisions and movement.
  • Revert — Means to go back to an earlier state on its own. "Reverse" implies an active force pushing something in the opposite direction.

In short: whenever you see "reverse" used as a verb, ask yourself — what was the current direction, order, or state of things? Whatever the answer, reversing means actively pushing against it and going the other way.
